A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MemoryBench study. The main text and complete appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, datasets, equations, tables, and figures can be matched despite additions and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, feedback comparisons, on-policy and stepwise experiments, and measurements of memory and inference time.

after.justification: v3 retains original system evaluations and additionally reports human feedback assessments, noise experiments, alternative-backbone comparisons, and a retrieval case study.

M1.justification: The Task Provider, User Simulator, and Performance Monitor framework, feedback prompts, and action-probability rules are retained. Expanded baseline descriptions, alternative backbones, and robustness experiments do not establish a change to the proposed default procedure.

E1.justification: The eleven source datasets, three domains, two languages, and four task formats remain. Coverage expands to human assessment of feedback and Legal-domain scenarios with altered user selectivity and noisy satisfaction signals. JRE-L/SciTechNews denotes retained coverage; MemoryBench-Full is introduced but explicitly not evaluated.

E2.justification: The eight LLMsys comparators and the action-feedback SFT baseline are retained. The new human study in A.2.5 adds professionally written human feedback as a comparator for simulated feedback. Adding MemBench to Table 1 is research positioning, not an evaluated system baseline.

E3.justification: A.1 changes the stated evaluation judge outside WritingBench from GPT-4o-mini to DeepSeek-V3. The reported LiSo Locomo sample count changes from 25 to 250 in v1 Table 6 versus v3 Table 9, without establishing an actual rerun. New protocols include a 200-task human comparison, two noise sweeps, and Mistral system/simulator controls on the Legal domain.

E4.justification: v1 already contains feedback ablations, learning trajectories, and timing analyses, which v3 largely retains. v3 substantially extends validation through human feedback assessment, selectivity and Gaussian-noise robustness tests, system/simulator backbone comparisons, and a Legal-domain case study examining retrieved memories and erroneous responses.

E5.justification: v3 Tables 13–14 introduce systematic mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting for the detailed off-policy results, whereas v1 reports point estimates. These deviations are across test examples. Table 7 additionally reports Fleiss' kappa for human judgments; neither addition establishes repeated experimental runs or run-based confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Aggregate and raw Qwen3-8B/32B results are extensively revised. For example, Open-domain Vanilla/BM25-M normalized scores change from 0.5259/0.5990 in v1 Table 7 to 0.6523/0.5720 in v3 Table 10. Changed evaluation settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains. Human win rates, noise responses, backbone comparisons, and case-study outcomes are also newly reported.

T1.justification: The continual-learning formulation in Section 2.1 and the logistic, binary, and copy-action probability rules in A.2.3 are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced; Gaussian perturbations specify an experimental condition.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: evaluating continual learning from simulated user feedback across diverse tasks and finding existing memory systems insufficiently effective and efficient. The additional experiments support these retained claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v3 newly interprets human ratings as feedback indistinguishability, noise sensitivity in terms of data quality versus coverage, and backbone controls as evidence that system design drives performance differences. It adds explanations involving irrelevant retrieved memories and a qualification about dataset imbalance in MemoryBench-Full. These substantially extend the interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v3 adds access information for MemoryBench-Full and Mistral-generated feedback, revises code/data pointers, explicitly states that Mem0g was not used, and clarifies that timing includes indexing and retrieval. Hardware, generation parameters, retrieval limits, and LoRA training settings were already documented in v1.

R1.justification: v3 adds MemBench by Tan et al. (2025) to the benchmark comparison and cites LLM-Evolve by You et al. (2024), distinguishing task-local conversational feedback from persistent feedback logs. These are limited additions to otherwise retained research positioning.

P1.justification: Most prose, section ordering, and prompt templates remain. v3 expands explanations of memory categories, baseline architectures, evaluation scope, and timing; adds appendix subsections for new analyses; standardizes JRE-L/SciTechNews naming; and edits author/header information.

P2.justification: v3 adds a memory-taxonomy illustration, dataset classification and human-assessment tables, two tables displaying standard deviations, three noise-analysis figures, and backbone-comparison and case-study tables. Existing displays are redistributed, and framework labels and the benchmark-comparison table are revised. This substantially expands the visual presentation beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the benchmark's central simulated-feedback component. Compared with v1's automated feedback-effect checks, A.2.5 adds direct human quality comparisons, while A.3.9–A.3.10 test feedback noise and backbone dependence; Tables 13–14 also expose variation across test examples. Low rater agreement and Legal-only robustness controls limit the strongest claims about human indistinguishability and backbone independence, but the complementary validation provides a substantial net improvement.
